full_text_en:
Eli Lilly and Company v. Jiangsu Hanssen Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. — Patent Infringement Dispute

[Ruling Summary]

When an expert appraisal institution, upon entrustment by a People's Court, conducts an appraisal of technical issues in dispute in a patent lawsuit, it shall base its appraisal on the authentic, lawful, and valid evidentiary materials that have been subject to cross-examination by the parties during court proceedings. An appraisal conclusion based on evidentiary materials that have not been cross-examined or verified by the parties is not lawful and valid evidence and cannot be used as a basis for ascertaining the facts of the case.

Civil Ruling of the Supreme People's Court

(2002) Min San Zhong Zi No. 8

Appellant (Plaintiff at First Instance): (USA) Eli Lilly and Company, domiciled at Indianapolis, Indiana, United States of America.

Legal Representative: Michael J. Muller, Deputy General Counsel of (USA) Eli Lilly and Company.

Agents ad litem: Ai Hong, attorney at Beijing Zhengjian Yongshen Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Wu Yuhe, attorney at Guangdong Huijun Law Firm.

Respondent (Defendant at First Instance): Jiangsu Hanssen Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd., domiciled at Lianyungang Economic and Technological Development Zone, Jiangsu Province.

Legal Representative: Cen Junda, Chairman of the Board of the company.

Agents ad litem: Ma Xiaogang, attorney at Beijing Haotian Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Wu Jingqing, attorney at Beijing Haotian Law Firm.

The Appellant, (USA) Eli Lilly and Company (hereinafter referred to as Eli Lilly), filed an appeal with this Court against the civil judgment (2001) Su Min San Chu Zi No. 001 rendered by the Jiangsu High People's Court in the case of a dispute over patent infringement with Jiangsu Hanssen Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. (formerly Lianyungang Hanssen Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd., hereinafter referred to as Hanssen). This Court lawfully formed a collegial panel composed of Jiang Zhipei, Presiding Judge and Chief Judge of the Third Civil Trial Division, Judge Dong Tianping, and Acting Judge Duan Lihong, and held a closed hearing of this case, with Court Clerk Li Jian keeping the record. The trial of this case is now concluded.

The court of first instance held that gemcitabine hydrochloride falls within the scope of new products as defined by the Patent Law, and Hanssen shall bear the burden of proof regarding its process for preparing gemcitabine hydrochloride. Given the particularities of this case, if the technical information concerning Hanssen's process were to be disclosed to Eli Lilly for review, it might cause unforeseeable and irreparable harm to Hanssen's commercial interests. Therefore, it was decided to adopt a modified method of cross-examination for the technical information of Hanssen's process: the information was not submitted to Eli Lilly for review but was instead submitted to an independent panel of expert appraisers to examine its authenticity and whether it was identical to the plaintiff's patented process. The appraisal materials submitted by the parties to the court for transmission to the appraisal body included: relevant documentation of Eli Lilly's three patents; a set of materials on the production methods for developing gemcitabine and gemcitabine hydrochloride provided to the court by Hanssen; a set of production materials submitted by Hanssen to the Jiangsu Provincial Drug Administration for the production of gemcitabine hydrochloride; and a set of materials for the new production process of gemcitabine hydrochloride submitted by Hanssen to the national drug regulatory authority starting in November 2001, along with relevant experimental spectra. Given that the appraisal conclusion found that Hanssen's improved process and the process submitted for production approval were different from the methods protected by the independent claims of Eli Lilly's patents, and the reasoning was very detailed, Eli Lilly's objections to the appraisal opinion were not sustainable, and there was insufficient contrary evidence to overturn the above appraisal conclusion. Therefore, this appraisal opinion should be used as valid evidence for deciding the case. Pursuant to this appraisal opinion, Hanssen's process for preparing gemcitabine hydrochloride (including the pilot-scale process and the process submitted for production approval) was not identical to the methods protected by the independent claims of Eli Lilly's three patents and did not fall within the scope of protection of the independent patent claims. Accordingly, Eli Lilly's lawsuit alleging patent infringement by Hanssen lacked factual and legal basis, and its claims should be dismissed. Pursuant to Article 59, Paragraph 1, and Article 60 of the Patent Law of the People's Republic of China (prior to amendment), the court rendered a judgment dismissing all claims of the plaintiff, Eli Lilly. The case acceptance fee of RMB 37,510 and the appraisal fee of RMB 25,000 were to be borne by Eli Lilly.

Dissatisfied with the judgment of first instance by the Jiangsu High People's Court, Eli Lilly appealed to this Court, arguing: 1. The court of first instance violated the provisions of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China and the Several Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Evidence in Civil Proceedings, depriving the appellant of its proper procedural rights by refusing to allow the appellant to review the evidence materials of the alleged infringement by the respondent during the first instance proceedings. The "facts" found in the judgment of first instance were not subject to cross-examination by the appellant. 2. The court of first instance, relying on its internal documents, designated the Jiangsu Provincial Department of Science and Technology as the appraisal body for this case, violating the Interim Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Judicial Appraisal Work. The appraisers had an interest in the respondent, the scope of appraisal was unclear, the evidence on which the appraisal opinion was based was contradictory, and the appraisal failed to recognize the basic inventive points of the appellant's patent. The appraisal conclusion lacked factual support. The appellant requested a retrial of this case and that all claims raised in the first instance be upheld.

The respondent, Hanssen, replied in defense, arguing: 1. The court of first instance clearly ascertained the facts. The respondent developed a process different from the appellant's patented process based on publicly available technical literature, which has already been verified through technical appraisal. 2. The Several Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Evidence in Civil Proceedings are not applicable to this case. A clear commercial competitive relationship exists between Eli Lilly and Hanssen. If Eli Lilly obtained Hanssen's trade secrets through the cross-examination procedure, it would inevitably cause unforeseeable and irreparable substantial losses to Hanssen's commercial interests. Pursuant to Article 66 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China and Article 72 of the Opinions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues concerning the Application of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the modified method adopted by the court of first instance did not infringe upon Eli Lilly's right to equal litigation. 3. The appraisal opinion was objective and truthful, and the court of first instance was not improper in using it as the basis for deciding the case.

This Court, upon trial, finds that Lianyungang Hanssen Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. was approved to change its name to Jiangsu Hanssen Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. on May 22, 2002. All evidentiary materials concerning the process for producing gemcitabine hydrochloride submitted by the respondent, Hanssen, to the court during the first instance were not provided to the appellant, Eli Lilly, for cross-examination. In the batch file (File No. 2001-10-252) concerning gemcitabine hydrochloride (submitted by Lianyungang Hanssen Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd.) currently held in the archives of the State Drug Administration, the following four pieces of evidence submitted by Hanssen to the court are not present: Research Materials and Literature on the New Production Process for Gemcitabine Hydrochloride (Attachment 1 of the Application Materials), Pilot-Scale New Process for Gemcitabine Hydrochloride (Attachment 2 of the Application Materials), HPLC Spectra for Intermediates, Products, and Pilot-Scale Products of the Small-Scale Test New Process for Gemcitabine Hydrochloride (Attachment 3 of the Application Materials), and Content and Basis for the Supplementary Application for Gemcitabine Hydrochloride (Application Materials). The respondent, Hanssen, claims that its process for producing gemcitabine hydrochloride involves trade secrets, but it has not clearly defined the specific scope of the alleged trade secrets.

This Court holds that, pursuant to Article 57, Paragraph 2 of the Patent Law of the People's Republic of China, the respondent, Hanssen, shall provide proof that its method for manufacturing the gemcitabine hydrochloride product is different from the patented method. Article 66 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China stipulates: "Evidence shall be presented in court and cross-examined by the parties." It further provides: "Evidence involving state secrets, trade secrets, or personal privacy shall be kept confidential. If it needs to be presented in court, it shall not be presented in an open session." These legal provisions grant the appellant, Eli Lilly, the procedural right to require the alleged infringer to effectively disclose complete evidentiary materials concerning the new product manufacturing method and to cross-examine them. They also grant the respondent the right to require the appellant to keep confidential the contents of the disclosed evidence that involve trade secrets. At the substantive level, these provisions fully consider the potential harm to the parties from disclosing trade secrets during litigation, providing effective protection for the parties' substantive civil rights and interests while safeguarding their legitimate procedural rights.

The technical process materials for preparing gemcitabine hydrochloride submitted by the respondent, Hanssen, which were requested to be kept confidential, should also be subject to cross-examination in accordance with the above legal provisions. Only on the basis of cross-examination of the evidence by both parties can a correct judgment be made as to whether the alleged infringing method is identical, equivalent, or different from the patented method. Therefore, during the trial of this case, this Court adopted a closed hearing session at the request of the respondent, Hanssen, and required the legal representative and agents ad litem of the appellant, Eli Lilly, as well as other participants in the proceedings, to assume a duty of confidentiality. They were prohibited from using the technical information belonging to Hanssen's trade secrets obtained through the litigation process for commercial purposes outside the litigation, subject to legal liability for any violation. The above method of cross-examination during the court hearing can both protect the appellant Eli Lilly's procedural right to lawfully obtain and cross-examine the evidentiary materials concerning the alleged infringing method and, at the same time, avoid the disclosure of Hanssen's alleged trade secrets due to the litigation process, thereby protecting Hanssen's legitimate interests. However, this Court's efforts during the second instance cannot remedy the procedural defects of the first instance.

When an expert appraisal institution, upon entrustment by a People's Court, conducts an appraisal of a disputed technical issue, it shall base its appraisal on the authentic, lawful, and valid evidentiary materials that have been subject to cross-examination by the parties during court proceedings. The four pieces of evidence submitted by the respondent, Hanssen, to the court, including the research materials and literature on the new production process for gemcitabine hydrochloride from its November 2001 supplementary application, were not archived in the batch file for gemcitabine hydrochloride at the State Drug Administration, and their authenticity could not be verified. All of the technical process materials concerning the respondent Hanssen's production of gemcitabine products submitted by the court of first instance to the appraisal body had not been subject to cross-examination by the parties, including the four literature materials, such as "Organic Chemistry," which Hanssen claimed were already publicly available. Therefore, the appraisal conclusion made by the appraisal institution based on evidentiary materials that had not been cross-examined or verified by the parties is not lawful and valid evidence and cannot be used as a basis for ascertaining the facts of this case. The court of first instance's dismissal of Eli Lilly's claims against Hanssen for patent infringement based on the appraisal conclusion constitutes unclear fact-finding.

In summary, the court of first instance admitted evidence that had not been subject to cross-examination by the parties, failed to protect the appellant Eli Lilly's legitimate procedural right to obtain technical information concerning the respondent Hanssen's method for producing the gemcitabine product that is different from the patented method, and used un-cross-examined evidence as the basis for entrusting the technical appraisal. This violates the provisions of the Civil Procedure Law that evidence must be subject to cross-examination in court before it can be used as the basis for deciding a case, leading to unclear fact-finding, insufficient evidence, and erroneous application of law in the judgment of first instance. Therefore, pursuant to Items (3) and (4) of Paragraph 1 of Article 153 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, this Court rules as follows:

1. The civil judgment (2001) Su Min San Chu Zi No. 001 of the Jiangsu High People's Court is vacated;

2. This case is remanded to the Jiangsu High People's Court for retrial.

Presiding Judge: Jiang Zhipei
Judge: Dong Tianping
Acting Judge: Duan Lihong

June 17, 2003

Court Clerk: Li Jian
